cards.title: Large-error approximate degree at logarithmic AC⁰ depth
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Does there exist an absolute constant A≥1 such that, for every real δ with 0<δ≤1/2, there are constants aδ>0, bδ>0, sδ≥1 and an integer Nδ≥2, and Boolean functions fδ,n:{−1,1}ⁿ→{−1,1} for every integer n≥Nδ, satisfying both of the following? First, fδ,n has an unbounded-fan-in AND/OR circuit of size at most n^{sδ} and depth at most ⌈A log₂(1/δ)⌉, with negations allowed at inputs. Second, deg_{εδ,n}(fδ,n)≥aδ n^{1−δ}, where εδ,n=1−2^{−bδ n^{1−δ}}. Here degε denotes the minimum total degree of a real polynomial that approximates the function with absolute error at most ε at every Boolean input. The same A must work for all δ; the other constants and the circuit family may depend on δ.
cards.why: Would determine whether the favorable depth dependence of strong AC⁰ polynomial lower bounds survives when approximation is allowed to be almost trivial, sharpening the relation between shallow circuits and weak randomized computation.
cards.status_note: Checked the full 2021 journal definitions and remaining question, the 2022 Bun–Thaler survey Section 8.3, and Sherstov’s expanded 2022 preprint Theorems 1.1–1.2 and Corollary 1.3 together with its June 2025 journal publication. The latter reaches inverse-polynomial rather than exponentially small advantage. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no resolution of the precise logarithmic-depth, exponentially-small-gap target; searches are not exhaustive.

progress.text: The FOCS precursor establishes near-linear constant-error approximate degree at depth O(log(1/δ)); the journal version appeared later.
Large-error near-linear lower bounds are obtained at depth O(1/δ), and the logarithmic-depth question is posed.
The full journal paper retains the logarithmic-depth question after discussing later threshold-degree and sign-rank results.

The journal version of Sherstov’s 2022 result gives depth-two near-linear bounds at constant error and inverse-polynomial advantage. Its Section 1.2 explicitly distinguishes that attainable error scale from smaller advantages.

This question allows error 1 minus an exponentially small quantity, while still demanding degree of order n^{1−δ}.

cards.definitions: For f:{−1,1}ⁿ→{−1,1} and 0≤ε<1, define degε(f)=min{deg(p): p∈ℝ[x₁,…,xₙ] and max_{x∈{−1,1}ⁿ}|p(x)−f(x)|≤ε}. Degree means total degree, the largest sum of exponents of a monomial with nonzero coefficient. Constants, including the zero polynomial, have degree zero by convention here. Coefficients may be arbitrary reals of arbitrary magnitude: no sparsity, coefficient-bit bound or boundedness away from the Boolean cube is imposed. Equivalently one may use multilinear polynomials, since restricting xᵢ²=1 on the cube does not increase degree. Approximation is worst case over all 2ⁿ inputs, not an average over a distribution. A circuit is a finite acyclic directed graph whose internal gates are AND or OR gates of arbitrary fan-in, whose input literals are xᵢ or their Boolean negations, and whose single output computes f under the usual identification of Boolean values with −1 and +1. Size counts internal gates; depth counts the maximum number of internal gates on an input-to-output path. Any polynomially equivalent gate/wire size convention gives the same existence question, since the polynomial exponent is unrestricted. The family is nonuniform: no algorithm for constructing its circuits or evaluating the polynomial coefficients is required. For each fixed δ its depth is independent of n and its size is polynomial in n, so it is in AC⁰. The question controls how that constant depth grows as δ decreases. Only A is uniform in δ; Nδ and the positive constants in the degree and error bounds need not be. Restricting δ to (0,1/2] records the small-δ asymptotic question and avoids a zero logarithm at δ=1. All sufficiently large input lengths are required, with constants chosen before n. The source’s Ω notation is expanded into aδ and bδ; the gap 1−εδ,n is exponentially small in n^{1−δ}. At error exactly 1 the zero polynomial approximates every ±1-valued function, so keeping a specified positive gap below 1 is essential. For comparison, threshold degree is the minimum degree of a polynomial p satisfying p(x)f(x)>0 at every input; it imposes no specified approximation gap and is a different measure.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove existence of a single absolute depth constant A and families with all the stated bounds for every 0<δ≤1/2, or prove the negation of that quantified existence statement. A result only at fixed approximation error, only at depth O(1/δ), or only for selected values of δ is insufficient. A negative answer must rule out arbitrary polynomial-size nonuniform families at the stated logarithmic depth, not merely one proposed construction.

context_blocks.title: Near-linear degree is known at larger depth
context_blocks.text: Bun and Thaler prove near-linear approximate-degree lower bounds even when error is exponentially close to the trivial value 1. Their depth grows proportionally to 1/δ. The question is whether the same degree and error regime can occur with depth only proportional to log(1/δ).

context_blocks.title: Constant error has a better depth dependence
context_blocks.text: Earlier work obtains degree Ω(n^{1−δ}) at depth O(log(1/δ)) for error 1/3. Allowing error extremely close to 1 can make polynomial approximation much easier, so that theorem does not establish the target here.

context_blocks.title: Depth-two results reach inverse-polynomial advantage
context_blocks.text: Sherstov’s STOC 2022 work, published in expanded journal form in 2025, proves near-linear approximate degree for polynomial-size constant-width DNF and CNF formulas. Its large-error theorem allows error 1/2−n^{-C} in the {0,1}-valued convention, for every fixed C; after rescaling to ±1 outputs this is 1−2n^{-C}. That gap is inverse polynomial, whereas this card demands an exponentially small gap. The theorem therefore does not resolve this question.

context_blocks.title: Threshold degree is a separate branch
context_blocks.text: The journal discussion includes Sherstov and Wu’s depth-k threshold-degree bound of order n^{(k−1)/(k+1)} up to logarithmic factors. It then asks separately for logarithmic-depth improvements for large-error approximate degree and for threshold degree. This card retains the large-error approximate-degree branch of the extracted question.

context_blocks.title: Why the error scale matters
context_blocks.text: The source connects this large-error regime to randomized query and communication models that charge both access cost and the logarithm of the inverse advantage over guessing. This makes the tradeoff meaningful even though the approximation advantage is very small.

cards.context:
Bun and Thaler prove near-linear approximate-degree lower bounds even when error is exponentially close to the trivial value 1. Their depth grows proportionally to 1/δ. The question is whether the same degree and error regime can occur with depth only proportional to log(1/δ).

Earlier work obtains degree Ω(n^{1−δ}) at depth O(log(1/δ)) for error 1/3. Allowing error extremely close to 1 can make polynomial approximation much easier, so that theorem does not establish the target here.

Sherstov’s STOC 2022 work, published in expanded journal form in 2025, proves near-linear approximate degree for polynomial-size constant-width DNF and CNF formulas. Its large-error theorem allows error 1/2−n^{-C} in the {0,1}-valued convention, for every fixed C; after rescaling to ±1 outputs this is 1−2n^{-C}. That gap is inverse polynomial, whereas this card demands an exponentially small gap. The theorem therefore does not resolve this question.

The journal discussion includes Sherstov and Wu’s depth-k threshold-degree bound of order n^{(k−1)/(k+1)} up to logarithmic factors. It then asks separately for logarithmic-depth improvements for large-error approximate degree and for threshold degree. This card retains the large-error approximate-degree branch of the extracted question.

The source connects this large-error regime to randomized query and communication models that charge both access cost and the logarithm of the inverse advantage over guessing. This makes the tradeoff meaningful even though the approximation advantage is very small.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
